competition: Hungarian National Secondary School Competition (OKTV), Mathematics Category III, Final

problems.problem: For an arbitrary non-right triangle, draw its orthic triangle, then the orthic triangle of that one, and so on (the vertices of the orthic triangle are the intersection points of the three altitude lines with the corresponding side lines). How many pairwise non-similar triangles are there whose angles, measured in degrees, are integers and for which the procedure sooner or later leads to a triangle similar to the original one?
About the positive integers $r$ and $s$ we know that for every positive integer $k$, $ks$ has at least as many divisors as $kr$. Prove that $r$ is a divisor of $s$.
The edge of a cube has length $n$ units. At most how many of the $6n^2$ unit squares forming its surface can be selected so that no two of them have a common side?
Prove that for every triangle $H$ there exists a line $e$ such that the reflection of $H$ in $e$ covers more than $3/4$ of the area of $H$.

Let $p_i$ denote the $i$-th prime, and let $Q_k = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_k$. (So, for example, $Q_4 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 210$.) Prove that among the numbers $1, 2, \dots, Q_k$ there are exactly $Q_k/2$ that are divisible by an odd number of the primes $p_1, \dots, p_k$.

The positive integers $n$ and $k$ are given, where $n \ge k + 2$. Further, let $A_1, \dots, A_m$ be $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set $H$ such that

(1) every one-element subset of $H$ is the intersection of some of the $A_i$; but

(2) if any one of the $A_i$ is omitted, (1) no longer holds.

(a) Show that $m \le kn$.

(b) Prove that with a suitable choice of the $A_i$, $m \ge kn - k^2$ can be achieved.

Every interior angle of the convex hexagon $A_1A_2 \ldots A_6$ is obtuse. The circles $k_i$ with centres $A_i$ $(1 \le i \le 6)$ are placed so that $k_1$ touches $k_2$ and $k_6$ externally, $k_2$ touches $k_1$ and $k_3$ externally, and in general $k_i$ touches $k_{i-1}$ and $k_{i+1}$ externally. The intersection point of the line joining the two points of tangency on $k_1$ and the line joining the points of tangency on $k_3$ is joined to $A_2$; this is the line $e$. Similarly, the intersection point of the lines joining the points of tangency on $k_3$ and on $k_5$ is joined to $A_4$; this is the line $f$. Finally, the intersection point of the lines joining the points of tangency on $k_5$ and on $k_1$ is joined to $A_6$; this is the line $g$. Show that $e$, $f$ and $g$ pass through one point.

Two players each have a pile of pebbles in front of them; initially both piles contain $k$ pebbles. First the first player adds a total of $2008$ new pebbles to these; he may distribute the new pebbles between the two piles arbitrarily (he may even put all of them into one pile). Then the second player adds a total of $2008$ new pebbles to the piles, and so on alternately. The winner is the player in whose pile (after his own move or after the opponent's move) the number of pebbles is a perfect square while this does not hold for the opponent's pile (if both piles are such, the game continues). Is it true that for infinitely many $k$ the second player has a winning strategy?

Show that for all numbers $1 < r < s < 2008/2007$ there exist positive integers $p$ and $q$ (not necessarily coprime) such that $r < p/q < s$ and the digit $0$ does not occur in the decimal representation of either $p$ or $q$.

Show that if $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ are arbitrary positive numbers, then at least one of
$$\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} 1/a_i = \infty \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_i/i^2 = \infty$$
holds. (For positive numbers $c_1, c_2, \dots$, $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} c_i = \infty$ means that the sums $s_k = c_1 + c_2 + \dots + c_k$ grow beyond all bounds as $k$ increases.)

Project the regular tetrahedron $ABCD$ orthogonally onto a number line lying in space, and let the projections of the vertices be the real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, respectively. Express the edge length of the tetrahedron in terms of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$.

One day a swarm of bees collected honey from the flowers of a particularly beautiful tree. Each bee visited the tree at most $100$ times, there were never more than two bees there at the same time, but any two bees met each other at the tree at some time. At most how many bees could the swarm have consisted of?

Prove that there are infinitely many right triangles whose side lengths are pairwise coprime integers and such that subtracting the length of either leg from the length of the hypotenuse gives a perfect cube.

The angles of the triangle $ABC$ are $\pi/7$, $2\pi/7$, $4\pi/7$. The angle bisectors of the triangle meet the opposite sides at the points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$. Show that the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is isosceles.
We want to cover completely the three faces meeting at one vertex of a cube with edge length $k$ using $k^2$ labels of size $3 \times 1$. For which $k$ can this be done?

The foot of the altitude from the vertex $C$ of the right triangle $ABC$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ is $D$. The angle bisector from the vertex $B$ meets the altitude $CD$ at the point $E$ and the leg $AC$ at the point $F$. Prove that $AD > 2 \cdot EF$.
Is there a positive integer among whose positive divisors there are $2011$ times as many perfect squares as perfect cubes?

Anna and Bálint play the following game: Anna draws an arbitrarily large empty graph (i.e. one without edges), then draws arbitrary edges one by one, which Bálint colours blue or red immediately after each is drawn. A further rule is that in the resulting graph every vertex may have degree at most $k$, and they agree on the value of $k$ in advance. What is the smallest $k$ for which Anna, playing cleverly, can certainly create a monochromatic path of length $2011$?

Let $n \ge 3$. In the $n$-member Liars' Club we ask everybody how many members of the club (other than himself) were born in the same year as he was. The club members all want to give false data in such a way that they give the answers $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in some order. About the actual years of birth we only know that they are not all different, but not all the same either. For which values of $n$ can we be sure that the club members can achieve their goal?

Let $B$ be an interior point of the segment $AC$. Draw the semicircles $k_1$ and $k_2$ on the segments $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, as diameters in the same half-plane. On the segment $BC$ as base, erect an isosceles triangle $BCD$ whose vertex $D$ lies on $k_2$. Let $K$ be the centre of the circle touching $k_1$, $k_2$ and the segment $BD$. Prove that $KB$ is perpendicular to $AC$.

Let $2 = p_1 < p_2 < \dots$ be the sequence of positive primes and
$$f(k, n) = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\left\lfloor n\sqrt{p_k/p_j} \right\rfloor.$$
Prove that for every integer $M > 0$ there is exactly one pair of positive integers $(k, n)$ for which $f(k, n) = M$.

(In the formula, $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the integer part of $x$, and $\sum$ denotes summation over the given indices; so for example $f(2, 1) = \lfloor 1 \cdot \sqrt{3/2} \rfloor + \lfloor 1 \cdot \sqrt{3/3} \rfloor = 2$ (the other terms of the sum are $0$).)

Three distinct circles $k$, $k_1$ and $k_2$ are given in the plane, with centres $O$, $O_1$, $O_2$ and radii $r$, $r_1$ and $r_2$, respectively. Suppose that $k$ touches $k_1$ internally at the point $E_1$, $k_2$ touches $k$ internally at the point $E_2 \ne E_1$, and the line $O_1O_2$ is perpendicular to the line $E_1E_2$. Express the radius $r$ in terms of $r_1$ and $r_2$.

Show that
$$\sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{m(m-1)(m-2)\ldots(m-k+1)k}{m^{k+1}} = 1.$$

Consider the sequences of length $n$ each of whose terms is $0$ or $1$. The sum of two such sequences is the result of termwise addition modulo $2$. For which positive integers $n$ can these sequences be arranged in pairs so that adding the two terms of each pair gives $2^{n-1}$ different sequences?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to the internal angle bisector at $B$, and from $B$ to the internal angle bisector at $A$. Denote the feet by $D$ and $E$, respectively. Prove that the line $DE$ meets the sides $AC$ and $BC$ of the triangle at the points where the incircle touches them.

For the positive numbers $p$ and $q$, $p + q \le 1$. Prove that for all positive integers $m$, $n$
$$(1 - p^m)^n + (1 - q^n)^m \ge 1.$$

From the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 2014^{2014}$, Aladár and Boglárka alternately delete one number (Aladár starts) until only two numbers remain. If the sum of the two remaining numbers is a perfect square, Boglárka wins; otherwise Aladár wins. Who has a winning strategy?

Through an external point of a circle $k$ a secant $e$ and two tangents are drawn; the points of tangency of the latter are $A$ and $B$. The line through the point $A$ parallel to $e$ meets $k$ also at a point $C$ different from $A$. Prove that the line $BC$ bisects the segment of $e$ lying inside $k$.

Suppose that for a finite set $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ and an infinite set $B = \{b_1 < b_2 < \dots\}$ of nonnegative integers, every nonnegative integer can be written uniquely in the form $a_i + b_j$. Show that then $B$ is necessarily "purely periodic", i.e. there exists $c > 0$ such that any nonnegative integer $b$ belongs to $B$ if and only if $b + c$ does.
Which polynomials $f$ with integer coefficients have the property that $f(2^j)$ is a positive prime power for every $j \ge 1$?
A subset of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ is called small if it is empty or has fewer elements than its smallest element. For a given $n$, how many small subsets are there?

Anna divides the numbers $n + 1, n + 2, \dots, n + 2k$ arbitrarily into $k$ disjoint pairs. Then she tells Balázs the product of the elements in each of the pairs. Let $f(n)$ be the largest $k$ for which Balázs can always find out from these $k$ product values the pairs Anna had in mind. Prove that there exist positive constants $c$ and $d$ independent of $n$ such that for every sufficiently large $n$
$$c\sqrt{n} < f(n) < d\sqrt{n}.$$

Points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ are taken on the sides of triangle $ABC$ opposite to $A$, $B$, $C$, respectively, so that the segments $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ pass through the same point $P$. Prove that
$$AP \cdot PA_1 + BP \cdot PB_1 + CP \cdot PC_1 < \frac{1}{3}\left(BC^2 + CA^2 + AB^2\right).$$

The sum of the integers $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{10}$ is $11$. At most how many integer solutions can the equation
$$a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \dots + a_{10}x^{10} = 1$$
in the unknown $x$ have?

An arbitrarily chosen interior point $P$ of a fixed acute triangle is reflected in all three side lines. Prove that there is exactly one point which, for every choice of $P$, lies in the triangle spanned by the reflections of $P$ as vertices.
Show that for every integer $k > 1$ there is a positive integer $m$ less than $k^2$ such that $2^m - m$ is divisible by $k$.

The planet Tatooine is famous for having two suns shining in its sky. Tatooine orbits the double star system consisting of the stars $A$ and $B$. The Force keeps the planet on a circular orbit which contains the segment $AB$ in its plane, whose centre is an interior point $C$ of the segment $AB$, and whose radius is greater than the distance $AB$. Given the points $A$, $B$, $C$ and the radius $r$ of the orbit, construct the point of the orbit from which the two suns appear in the sky of Tatooine at the largest possible angular distance from each other.

Let $p \ge 1$ be an integer. On a circle of unit circumference, $p$ points are coloured red so that on the two sides of any diameter line of the circle not passing through a red point, the numbers of red points differ by at most $100$. Prove that the sum of the circular distances of any point of the circle from the red points is at least $(p/4) - 25$. (The circular distance of two points is the arc length of the shorter of the two arcs joining them.)

Is it true that for every natural number $k$ there exists a $k$-element set of positive integers such that in every nonempty subset the sum of the elements is a perfect power? (A number is called a perfect power if it can be written in the form $a^q$, where $a$ and $q$ are natural numbers and $q \ge 2$.)

The sides $BC$ and $CD$ of the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ are equal. Let $E$ be the reflection of the point $B$ in the point $C$. Show that the reflection of the intersection point of the diagonals in the line $BC$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABE$.

Let $f$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients, $k \ge 2$ an integer, and $p$ a prime. Suppose that the numbers $f(0), f(1), \dots, f(p-1)$ give $k$ different remainders when divided by $p$. Prove that then the degree of $f$ is at least $(p-1)/(k-1)$.
$7$ vectors are given in space so that no three of them lie in one plane. Show that if we take the scalar product of any two different ones, we get at least three different numbers.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on the positive halves of the $x$- and $y$-axes, respectively, of a Cartesian coordinate system with origin $O$. Let $P$, $A$ and $B$ be lattice points in the interior of the first quadrant such that the ray $PA$ has direction $OX$, the ray $PB$ has direction $OY$, and $PA = PB$. Prove that if there is a lattice point $A'$ on the ray $PA$ for which the angle $AOP$ equals the angle $XOA'$, then there is also a lattice point $B'$ on the ray $PB$ for which the angle $BOP$ equals the angle $YOB'$.

Let the finite graph $G$ be a tree with $n \ge 2$ vertices. Prove that the vertices of $G$ can be numbered from $1$ to $n$ so that for every vertex the sum of the numbers of its neighbours gives a different remainder upon division by $n$ than the number of the vertex itself.

Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be polynomials with real coefficients and leading coefficient $1$. Show that if the sets of their values at the integers are the same, then there is an integer $k$ such that either $g(x) = f(x + k)$ for every real $x$, or $g(x) = f(-x + k)$ for every real $x$.

Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$, respectively. Let the feet of the altitudes of the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ from $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ on the opposite side lines be $A_2$, $B_2$, $C_2$, respectively. Prove that the lines $AA_2$, $BB_2$, $CC_2$ pass through one point.
Which polynomials with integer coefficients have the property that for every prime $p$, all possible remainders modulo $p$ occur among their values at the integers?

Let $F_0, F_1, \dots$ be the Fibonacci sequence, defined by the initial values $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and for $i \ge 2$ by the recursion $F_i = F_{i-1} + F_{i-2}$. Consider the polynomial $p$ of degree at most $2020$ for which
$$p(0) = F_0, \ p(1) = F_1, \ \dots, \ p(2020) = F_{2020}.$$
Determine the value of $p(2021)$.

Choose finitely many chords in a circle and colour them red or blue in such a way that the same number of red chords as blue chords end at every point of the circle. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point of the circle, and consider the distances of $P$ from the lines of the chords. Prove that the product of the distances belonging to the red chords equals the product of those belonging to the blue ones.

James Bond, agent 007, has to obtain a secret list consisting of distinct five-digit numbers, which he must deliver to M (the order of the numbers does not matter; the list contains at least $10$ and at most $100$ numbers). However, the courier is suspected of being an enemy agent, so Bond changes one number of the list so that it is still a five-digit number different from the others. Can Bond and M agree in advance (without knowing the secret list) on a method by which M can reconstruct the original list from the modified one?

Consider all polynomials $f(x, y)$ in two variables with integer coefficients for which $f(x, y) = f(y, x)$ identically, and $f(m, n) = 0$ for all integers $m$ and $n$ with $0 \le m, n \le 2021$. What is the smallest positive value among the values $f(2022, 2022)$ as $f$ ranges over all such polynomials?
Prove that in every triangle the distance of the incentre from the centroid is less than one third of the longest side of the triangle.

Let $a_0$ be an arbitrary integer and consider the sequence defined by the recursion $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 + 1$ $(n \ge 0)$. Show that the numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots$ together have infinitely many different prime divisors.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n, b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ be positive integers such that the fractions
$$\frac{a_1}{b_1}, \frac{a_2}{b_2}, \dots, \frac{a_n}{b_n}$$
are pairwise distinct. Prove that
$$(a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n)(b_1 + b_2 + \dots + b_n) \ge \frac{n^3}{16}.$$

At most how many points with integer coordinates can be given in space so that each of them is at the same distance from the origin, and any two of them together with the origin form triangles of equal area?

Some children from a housing estate attend clubs. Among the participants of the clubs there are both boys and girls, every boy attends exactly $p$ clubs and every girl exactly $q$ clubs, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers, and any boy-girl pair attends at most one common club. We also know that for any two clubs, more boys attend the first than the second if and only if more girls attend the first than the second. At least how many clubs must there be? (Give the answer as a function of $p$ and $q$.)

Let $k$ and $\ell$ be positive integers, $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_k$ and $b_1 \le b_2 \le \dots \le b_\ell$ positive integers, and finally let $q(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree at least one. Suppose that for every positive integer $n$, $a_1^n + a_2^n + \dots + a_k^n + q(n)$ divides $b_1^n + b_2^n + \dots + b_\ell^n + q(n)$. Prove that then $k = \ell$ and $a_i = b_i$ for every $1 \le i \le k$.

In the acute triangle $ABC$, let $D$, $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. Let $k$ be the circle that passes through $C$ and touches the side $AB$ at the point $F$, and let $\ell$ be the circle that passes through $B$ and touches the side $AC$ at the point $E$. Suppose that the circles $k$ and $\ell$ meet at two points, $M$ and $N$. Prove that if the line $MN$ is reflected in the point $D$, the resulting line passes through $A$.

$30$ lamps and some switches are given. A subset of the lamps is assigned to each switch. When we use a switch, all lamps in the subset belonging to it change state, i.e. those that were on are switched off and those that were off are switched on. Initially all lamps were off. We know that for every lamp there is a switch to which the lamp is assigned. Determine the largest number $k$ such that, however the switches work, one can certainly have $k$ lamps on at the same time.

Solve the following system of equations over the real numbers:
$$x^{2023} + y^{2023} + z^{2023} = 3,$$
$$x^{2025} + y^{2025} + z^{2025} = 3,$$
$$x^{2027} + y^{2027} + z^{2027} = 3.$$

The circle $k$ touches the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ externally at $C$. Let $a$, $b$ denote the lengths of the sides $BC$, $CA$ of the triangle, respectively, and let $a_1$ and $b_1$ be the lengths of the tangent segments drawn from $A$ and from $B$, respectively, to $k$. Prove that $a_1 : b_1 = b : a$.

Is it true that there exist two different positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that for every integer $0 \le i \le 2026$, $a + i$ and $b + i$ are products of exactly the same number of (not necessarily distinct) prime factors?

A badminton club has $n \ge 4$ members. During their annual tournament they play doubles matches so that any two pairs without a common member play each other exactly once. After a match, each member of the winning pair gets one point, and the members of the losing pair get no points. For which $n$ is it possible that at the end of the tournament every member of the club has the same number of points? (There are no draws in badminton.)
